Self and Ego: A Framework for their Integration

Irene Fast PHD

Irene Fast

580 Union Drive
Ann Arbor, MI 48109

Irene Fast  

The place of the self in relation to the ego has posed continuing, thorny problems for psychoanalytic psychology. Theoretical elaborations of the self in relation to objects, and of the ego in relation to the id and superego, have taken such different courses that they have formed discrete perspectives within psychoanalysis—the object relations and structural models, respectively. In the object relations framework, the self is seen to originate in early interactive experiences in which the infant does not differentiate self from others, and to develop by the differentiation of self and object structures into increasingly complex and integrated wholes distinct from one another.1 The ego of the structural model arises from id experiences: the infant is sensitive only to its own bodily processes, remains oblivious to the environment, and develops beyond this stage as the ego brings the influences of reality to bear on the id. To account for early adaptation to the environment, ego psychological elaborations of the structural model, following Hartmann (1939), add a conflict-free line of development not based on the drives.

Each perspective has particular areas of conceptual weakness that make clear its need of the other.

Dr. Fast is Professor of Psychology, University of Michigan.

1It is beyond the scope of this paper to discuss the many variations in psychoanalytic object relations theories. The formulation used here appears to be central to such frameworks, one that is generally familiar and commonly used in clinical discussions.141

Epilogue

Arthur Malin Issue Editor

Arthur Malin

Arthur Malin  

The preceding papers cover a wide range of concerns in the conversion of psychotherapy to psychoanalysis. A method of study of the problem was described. Resistances to psychoanalysis on the part of both the patient and the analyst were examined. There was a discussion of patients originally considered unsuitable for psychoanalysis, who became suitable with psychotherapy, and a case example was given. The idea that the original psychotherapy can be similar to the beginning of any analytic process was considered. Some of the assumptions regarding the nature of the psychoanalytic process which have a bearing on conversion were questioned.

The contributors accept the proposition that the conversion of psychotherapy to psychoanalysis is a legitimate endeavor, even with the same therapist, and is not necessarily doomed to failure. The survey of the institutes of the American Psychoanalytic Association indicated that conversion is now relatively routine for required supervisory cases for candidates.

Conversion of psychotherapy to psychoanalysis has clearly become a common procedure. The contributions to this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry have sought to expand our understanding of the process. The change might well be based on economic considerations and the availability of cases, or perhaps on the widening scope; in any event, the overall direction seems to be toward approving conversion to analysis with the same therapist.

In Memoriam

Joseph Lichtenberg Editor-in-Chief

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Dr. Nathaniel J. London died on October 10, 1989. Psychoanalytic Inquiry lost one of its most valued and productive editors, and I lost a cherished friend and fraternity brother from college days. Death does not “become” a person as full of life, of ideas and enthusiasm as Nat. Nat cared a lot about a lot of things—his family, psychoanalysis, his creative output, and, as a writer, choosing just the right word. Two of his contributions are, I believe, pivotal points in orienting psychoanalytic thinking: his explication of two theories of schizophrenia in “An Essay on Psychoanalytic Theory” (1973, Int. J. Psychoanal., 54: 169-193), the link between play and the transference neurosis in “The Play Element of Regression in the Psychoanalytic Process” (1981, Psychoanal. Inq., 1: 7-28). At the time of his death, Nat was considering editing an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry on play and humor—a topic most befitting our memory of him.

Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

During the last two decades the formulations and models of object relations have dramatically influenced the theory and practice of psychoanalysis. Beginning in the late 60s, the writings of Kernberg (1975) and Modell (1976) introduced to many psychoanalysts in the United States the ideas of the British School of object relations in conceptualizing therapeutic action, interaction, narcissism, and formulations of the self.

Interest in object relations was further embellished by additional developments within psychoanalysis. Mahler described the infant's immersion in symbiotic fusion and a gradual separation-individuation into selfhood. Self psychology, introduced by Kohut and his followers, conceptualized the centrality of the self in the psychoanalytic model and the value of the selfobject as an interactive extension of the self in maintaining the integrity of the self. Data derived from infant observation suggested an interactive loop between mother and infant as the basic motivational configuration and not a drive-motivated force. Furthermore, the burgeoning literature on the psychoanalytic treatment of severe pathological states (Kernberg, 1975; Pao, 1979; Frosch, 1983) focused on formulation of deficiencies and conflict linked to early object relations.

Recently, an entire issue of the Psychoanalytic Quarterly

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

The questions raised in this issue when considered as a whole present a challenge to the reader. Each contributor attempts to synthesize object relations formulations with the classic psychoanalytic model. The result is an illumination of many of the areas within psychoanalysis that are incomplete and require refinement.

Fast described the problem of integrating the structural dynamic and representational points of view, borrowing a model from Piaget's theory of development.

Sandler focused on internalization in his continued work on clarifying the internalized object and internalized object relations. Moreover, he addressed the problem of how to conceptualize the relationship between the self and its internal and external objects.

Modell emphasized the problem of the dichotomy between attachment, safety, and instinctual discharge as different [principles of] sources of motivation.

Bacal emphasized the need to extend self psychology into an object relations theory and, thus, more readily able to accommodate concepts of resistance, transference, defense, and fantasy formation.

Finally, Krystal described the weakness of the drive/conflict model as a conceptualization of psychic deficiency and argues for the information process model.

Psychoanalysis as a theory of the mind and as a model of treatment requires a constant influx of ideas to enable its refinement and sophistication.

Epilogue

Ernest Wolf Issue Co-Editor

Ernest Wolf

Ernest Wolf  

When, in 1954, the journal of the american psychoanalytic association brought together what Wallerstein calls “the ferment” and the “rival camps” evoked by Alexander's innovative concept of the corrective emotional experience, Alexander could open his essay by staing, “Concerning the essential nature of the treatment there seems to be little disagreement among psychoanalysts today” (1954, p. 685). Did he really mean this or was he just putting a good face on a bad situation? This statement has puzzled me because what I thought I saw when I came to Chicago in 1955 was disagreement intense enough to be followed shortly by Alexander's move to the West Coast.

“The Corrective Emotional Experience Revisited” promised to be a theme that would bring into the open the differences and the similarities with which psychoanalysts of diverse theoretical persuasions from within the English-speaking world approach their clinical task of conducting psychoanalytic treatment today. We had hoped that a fresh look at old disputes might bring out more clearly how different psychoanalytic theoretical conceptualizations translate into controversially different clinical technical recommendations. Though the heat of the controversies of the 40s and 50s indeed seems mostly to have dissipated, one can hardly claim to find a general acceptance of Alexander's ideas among contemporary psychoanalysts. To be sure, all of our contributors agree on the essential importance of an analysand's emotional experience of the relationship with the analyst.

The basis for the unpopularity of the concept of the corrective emotional experience is that Alexander recommended that the analyst vary his behavior in order to accentuate the discrepancy between the transference and the “reality” of the analyst's behavior or personality. Precisely where he makes this recommendation is unclear; most of his comments are along the lines of the “analyst assumes an attitude different from that which the parent had assumed toward the child in the original conflict situation” (Alexander & French, 1946, p. 66). For example, the neutral, accepting, and calm stance of the psychoanalyst runs counter to the stance taken by the symptomatic, traumatic, or conflicted parent.

In essence, a corrective emotional experience is achieved when the original traumatic conflict is reactivated in the clinical transference and worked through by the patient's experiencing the discrepancy between what is expected of the analyst and the reality.

Discussion

Jay Greenberg PHD

Jay Greenberg

275 Central Park West, 1BB
New York, N. Y. 10024,

Jay Greenberg  

When he talked about repression, Freud occasionally compared unconscious impulses to an unruly, uninvited stranger clamoring to get into a respectable gathering. Barring his admission once wouldn't be enough, Freud warned; “three or four … strong men” would have to guard the door against subsequent attempts (1910, p. 25). For many years, relational thinking, like that boisterous intruder, has been trying to crash the party of classical psychoanalysis.

Wily and persistent intruders, relational concepts have appeared in many guises and have relied on a range of tactics to get through the gates. From the “more Freudian than thou” polemic of Melanie Klein, to the brash confrontations of Sullivan's interpersonal psychiatry, to “just adding where the theory has gaps” approach of Mahler and the early Kohut, it has become apparent over time that relational thinking simply will not go away. But until recently, for each attempt there have been at least three or four strong men (and women) to block entry effectively.

Now, I think, it is time to declare the struggle over. There is a solid and growing consensus that the theory of object relations is central at least to what we do as psychoanalysts. Perhaps (although more controversial) there is even consensus that relational sensibilities are an essential facet of a psychoanalytic vision of the human condition.

Dr. Greenberg is Faculty and Supervising Analyst, William Alanson White Institute; Faculty and Supervising Analyst, Post-Doctoral Program in Psychoanalysis, New York University.

Conversion of Psychotherapy to Psychoanalysis: The Policies of the Institutes of the American

G. Pigman PHD

G. Pigman

California Institute of Technology 104-40
Pasadena, CA 91125

G. Pigman  

Analysts trained as recently as a decade ago recall being discouraged or even prohibited from converting patients they had been seeing in psychotherapy into psychoanalytic control cases. Today one often hears that a decline in the numbers of patients presenting themselves for analysis has led to a change in the practices of many analysts, who now start patients in once-or twice-a-week therapy and then convert them to analysis. Moreover, the American Psychoanalytic Association has made its acceptance of conversion more explicit, although this position does not appear to be as well known as it should be. To learn more about their current policies I made a survey of the institutes of the American concerning conversion. The results may be useful, since at least one institute does not realize that the American looks more favorably on conversion now than in the past.

I asked the chairmen of the education committees whether their institutes allow control cases to be converted, what conditions govern conversion, and whether their policies have changed over the past 10 to 20 years. All of the institutes that responded to my inquiries — 24 of the 26 — allow conversion.

Dr. Pigman is Associate Professor of Literature, California Institute of Technology, and a graduate of the Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute.

Prologue and Proposals

Because modern neuroscience has amassed evidence that associative, representational, and affective processes are all biological phenomena, one may now begin to view conflict as the learned association of a mental representation (of anything) and one or more of the several identificable dysphoric affects — for example, anxiety/fear, embarrassment/shame, sadness/depression, or disgust (Kandel, 1983, 1985; Reiser, 1984, 1985; Schwartz, 1987, 1988a, b 1990).

In this model of “conflict,” the fundamental units of human character disturbance consist significantly not of deficits but of representations associated too tightly with dysphoric feelings of often inappropriate intensity; this paradigm erases any fundamental conceptual distinction between, for example, “drive”-focused and narcissistic or “self”-related psychopathology: the registrations of either sexual excitement or the contours of one's face may, one can suggest, become linked with equal plausibility — and, very possibly, through similar neurophysiological mechanisms — with anxiety, shame, depression, or disgust.

Dr. Schwartz is a member of the Faculty, Department of Psychiatry, Office of Training and Standards, D.C. Commission on Mental Health Services, St. Elizabeths Hospital, Washington, D.C.

Prologue

Jule Miller Issue Editor and Stephen Post Issue Editor

Stephen Post

Stephen Post  

Agreat deal of interest was stimulated by a previous issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry (Vol. 7) entitled “Models of the Mind: Perspectives on a Clinical Study.” For that inquiry, prominent analysts representing various schools of thought were asked to examine the process notes of analytic sessions conducted by an established analyst with a traditional orientation.

The present issue is a continuation of that study using a different analytic perspective. The clinical material consists of four consecutive analytic sessions conducted by an established analyst working from a self psychological orientation. We are very fortunate that James L. Fosshage, Ph.D., has been willing to contribute the clinical protocol. Dr. Fosshage is a member of the National Council for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology and is widely respected by his fellow self psychologists for his capacities as a clinician, teacher, and researcher. Our contributors, each selected because he or she was a distinguished exemplar of an important position in psychoanalysis, prepared their discussions independently.

Our invitation to our contributors was similar to that given the contributors to the earlier study: examine the clinical material, describe their understanding of it from their particular perspectives, and indicate the kinds of interventions and technical approaches that might follow from that understanding. Such a format probably tends to emphasize differences more than similarities among the various contributors, as well as between the commentators and the reporting analyst.

The Emotional Position of the Analyst in the Shift from Psychotherapy to Psychoanalysis

Alan Skolnikoff MD

Alan Skolnikoff

205 Edgewood Avenue
San Francisco, CA 94117

Alan Skolnikoff  

When the question of converting from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis arises, the focus ordinarily is on the patient—especially the patient's capacity or readiness for the change. My focus, in contrast, is on the analyst's state of mind when confronting this circumstance. And because the analyst does live in the real world and is affected by it, it seems reasonable to start with a few observations on the external factors impinging on him or her.

The most conspicuous of these is the change in the general attitude of the public and broad mental health community toward psychoanalysis viewed in comparison to psychotherapy. It is not necessary to compare the current climate of opinion with that of the midcentury when psychoanalysis was the treatment of choice for anyone with the necessary time, money, and patience and when patients undergoing all sorts of therapy referred to their “analyses.” We need only compare today's climate with that of a decade or so ago to find differences in the way both analysts and patients feel about analysis.

Dr. Skolnikoff is Training and Supervising Analyst, San Francisco Psychoanalytic Institute, and Associate Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, University of California, San Francisco.

J. Burland  

Our topic is how our theories shape our psychoanalytic technique, and Dr. Fosshage is to be thanked for presenting clinical material that allows for such an exercise. I will initially be more specific about our points of divergence, although we have points of convergence as well; the purpose of this exercise is, after all, to focus on what distinguishes one set of theories from another, and how these differences affect technique.

We seem most to differ in the general area of to what extent the analyst is what has been called a “real new object” and to what extent he or she is a transference object. Implicit in this contrasting point of view is another; namely, is Dr. Fosshage's patient best understood as suffering from a deficiency or a conflict disorder. The theories that support the clinical concept of deficiency disorder go hand in hand with placing an emphasis on the analyst as a real new object whose empathic attunement compensates for the previous empathic failures of the primary objects. By contrast, another set of internally consistent concepts would hold that the empathic failures of the primary objects create ego structural malformations, conflicts, and compromise formations; that these are later played out in life as well as in the various narcissistic transferences in which the initial insult with its resultant means of responding are reenacted.

Robert Stolorow PHD

Robert Stolorow

11726 San Vicente Blvd.
Suite 410
Los Angeles, CA 90049

Robert Stolorow  

Underlying any consideration of the question of converting psychotherapy to psychoanalysis is a set of assumptions about what constitute the defining features that distinguish psychoanalysis from other modes of therapy. In this paper, I examine four such assumptions — or, as I prefer to call them, myths — about the essential nature of a psychoanalytic process.

1. The Myth of the Neutral Analyst

It is widely assumed that one feature distinguishing psychoanalysis from other therapies is the analyst's consistent adherence to a stance of “technical neutrality.” Indeed, according to Kernberg (Panel, 1987), it is the degree of the psychotherapist's deviation from technical neutrality that will determine the ease with which successful conversion to psychoanalysis can be achieved: the more neutral the therapist, the easier the shift will be (p. 720). But how is such neutrality to be defined? And does it really exist?

Dr. Stolorow is a member of the faculty of the Southern California Psychoanalytic Institute and a member of the core faculty of the Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity.

Stephen Mitchell PHD

Stephen Mitchell

251 West 71st Street, #1B
New York, NY 10023

Stephen Mitchell  

I am designating my perspective “relational” because it is grounded in the traditions of interpersonal psychoanalysis and British school object relations theories. Purists in either of these two schools of thought tend to regard the other as quite foreign. “Classical” interpersonalists, following Sullivan, tend to focus on what people do and largely eschew intrapsychic concepts concerning what is taken to be the latent structure of experience. This approach is at considerable odds with the language and sensibility of the British school and its Kleinian-derived emphasis on phantasy and “primitive” mental processes. On the other hand, various advocates of “object relations theory” tend to value explanations having to do with the earliest relationship between the infant and the mother, a far cry from the “here-and-now,” interactional focus of much interpersonal theory. Nevertheless, I discovered a number of years ago that my own clinical and theoretical perspective had taken shape in the interaction of these influences, along with certain strains from both existential psychoanalysis and revisionist versions of “Freudian” theory (particularly those of Loewald and Schafer). Since such an approach seems to fit into no preexisting category, I am using relational to encompass this mixture of influences (see Mitchell, 1988).

Dr. Mitchell is Training and Supervising Analyst, William Alanson White Institute; Faculty and Supervisor, New York University Postdoctoral Program.

Some Comments on the Alexander Technique

Hanna Segal MD

Hanna Segal

50 Eton Court
Eton Avenue
London NW3 3HJ ore

Hanna Segal  

It is not easy for me to comment on Alexander's technique since I have no first-hand experience of that technique; nor have I ever had discussions with anyone using it. Such knowledge as I have comes from some reading and some contacts with patients who had been treated according to it. I have, however, had some experience of discussions with analysts using a variety of active techniques, and some of my disagreements are with active techniques, usually derived from Ferenczi, in general.

I am in agreement with some of Alexander's criticism of the classical technique. I certainly agree with him that an analyst is not a neutral mirror onto which the patient in phantasy transfers his past objects, and I agree with him that such a neutral attitude is not possible in reality, nor would it be desirable if it were.

I also agree with him, and indeed it is a general psychoanalytical tenet, that psychoanalysis is a corrective emotional experience and that purely intellectual insight produces no changes. Certainly now increasingly greater emphasis is put by analysts and, I think, classical analysts as well as the so-called object relations school, on the nature of object relationships, and I doubt if anyone today holds totally to the view criticized by Alexander.

Dr. Segal is Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatry and a member of the British Psychoanalytic Society.

Paul Ornstein MD

Paul Ornstein

4177 Rose Hill Avenue
Cincinnati, OH 45229

Paul Ornstein  

The evolution of a psychoanalytic process is codetermined by what each participant brings to it. Hence, the analyst is ever mindful of letting the patient's contribution emerge as spontaneously as possible. Looking at this process rather grossly, we may perhaps still agree with Freud that, just as in a chess game, only the opening and closing moves are well defined; while those in between are of an endless, unpredictable variety. Still, we often speak of a “standard procedure”—which exists only if we look at the psychoanalytic process in a very distant and highly abstract way. When we examine any sample of this process under the microscope, however, neither the chess-game analogy (except for the in between phase with its endless variety), nor the idea of a “standard procedure” holds true. Any entry into a psychoanalysis — as well as the full journey through it — is always highly idiosyncratic for both participants, no matter how we may generalize about these entries. On this microscopic level there is nothing “standard” or “well defined” about the precise conduct of an analysis, because no two analyses are ever alike, even if they are not haphazard and have their definite, well-articulated general “rules.

James Fosshage  

At the beginning of treatment, the patient, whom I will refer to as P,1 was 28 years old, had been married for several years, and was the mother of a young son. She had just terminated a previous psychoanalysis of three years duration with a different analyst that had initially helped to bring about some order in her life by curtailing the use of drugs, alcohol, and promiscuous behavior. However, during the last year of that analysis, P had become increasingly depressed. Her depressive episodes seemed to be precipitated by the sessions themselves, dissipating between sessions, but extending in duration until finally depression became a chronic state. The most salient problematic theme in regard to this former analysis which emerged in our initial consultation was that P needed desperately and apparently frequently requested, if not demanded, to know that her analyst “cared” about her. The analyst was allegedly stalwart in not responding. In response to P's relentless insistence, the analyst reportedly resorted to the interpretation that an open expression of caring on her part would be of no help to her, intimating that P would not believe her. Experiencing this interpretation as yet another evasive maneuver, P angrily retorted that the analyst was a “walking corpse.” This episode appeared to epitomize the therapeutic impasse that led to the termination of treatment.

Dr. Fosshage is Co-founder, Board Director, and Faculty, National Institute for the Psychotherapies, New York City. He is a member of the Core Faculty, Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity, New York City and also a Faculty member and Supervisor, New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis.

The Analyst's Response

James Fosshage PHD

James Fosshage

330 West 58th Street
New York, NY 10019

James Fosshage  

The impact of psychoanalytic theories on analytic understanding and technique is most evident in comparative responses to a detailed clinical study. Each discussant has assessed and organized the clinical material from his/her vantage point. Espousing and proving one's particular constructions resulted in very disparate readings of the patient's experience and of the analyst's premises and subjective experiences. Clearly, with the plurality of psychoanalytic theories differences abound.

For purposes of comparing and contrasting the various clinical approaches to the material I will address the premises of the discussants and assess, from my perspective, their constructions of the clinical material. In the comparison I will also further elucidate my understanding and approach to the clinical experience. Space constrictions require me to focus succinctly on specific highlights of each discussion.

First, I will schematically present the model of therapeutic action fundamental to my understanding and technique. Because the functions of the transference dimension of idealization were addressed and understood so differently by the discussants, I will compare the various approaches to idealization under that heading. And I will discuss under a separate heading my “nonstandard” response in the “Cadillac” incident because it elicited strong reactions.

My general orientation within psychoanalysis is self psychological. However, no orientation is uniform, and wide divergences exist among those who claim a similar orientation.

Motivation for Psychoanalysis and the Transition from Psychotherapy

Stephen Bernstein MD

Stephen Bernstein

146 Wallis Road
Chestnut Hill, MA 02167

Stephen Bernstein  

The motivation necessary for a patient to accept the recommendation to enter psychoanalysis depends on a sufficient, ongoing level of distress experienced as internal, and the capacity to view an analyst as psychically safe and analysis as potentially leading to relief. In this paper I focus on the appropriate role of the analyst as psychotherapist in fostering such motivation and the process of its evolution.

Some factors that tend to foster the motivation for psychoanalysis include knowledge of its availability and potential benefits; an accepting external environment to support its conduct; the awareness that one's responses to external stresses are related to longstanding internal neurotic distress; and some experience of temporary relief and controllable regression obtained with an interested consultant, psychotherapist, or psychoanalyst.

The experienced clinician will recognize the process I describe as one that naturally involves establishing a treatment environment in which the patient's awareness is focused on his internal experience and conflict, and in which he can experience a safe and reversible regression. In this treatment environment the patient's motivation for analysis can be assessed and resistances to analysis can be voiced and explored.

Dr. Bernstein is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, and Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Tufts University School of Medicine.

An Information Processing View of Object-Relations

Henry Krystal MD

Henry Krystal

26011 Evergreen, #206
Southfield, MI 48076

Henry Krystal  

In 1914, as Freud was studying melancholia by comparing it to the universally known human reaction of mourning, he became involved in proposing two models of object relations. One was based on the physics and physiology of his age, the other was influenced by his recent work “Totem and Taboo” (1913), which inspired his extraordinary fantasy-making power by leading him to consider the religious practices of people he had read about who managed to deny the conscious recognition of the loss of their loved ones by developing rituals which represented cannibalistic fantasies. Freud was inspired to make a generalization which has become a pillar of psychoanalysis that still stands. It is that the only way the ego can “give up” any object is by introjecting it. He erroneously assumed that we psychologically and unconsciously cannibalize our lost objects after we introject them into the ego. The object continues its existence within us, just like the duck inside the bad wolf that swallowed her, or like Pinocchio inside the whale.

To this day most analysts say that we introject our lost objects after we lose them. Every once in a while, a medical student (never a psychoanalytic candidate) inquires: “If we introject the lost love objects after they're gone — where were they all the time till then?”

Dr. Krystal is Professor of Psychiatry, Michigan State University; Lecturer, Michigan Psychoanalytic Institute.

Priscilla Roth BA and Hanna Segal MD

Hanna Segal

12 Parkhill Road

Hanna Segal  

We are pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this colloquium, and we thank Dr. Fosshage for making available to us such detailed clinical material. We are acutely aware of the difficulties involved in an analysis being presented in such detail, but, like Dr. Fosshage, we believe that only by looking closely at what goes on from moment to moment within a session — looking at the raw data and not at the analyst's summary after the event — can we effectively discuss our different points of view. We are grateful to Dr. Fosshage for making this possible.

The material itself is extremely interesting and seems particularly well suiied to demonstrate the way current events both within and outside of the analysis get woven, along with dreams and memories and associations, into a rich transference relationship in which the patient's central difficulties and disturbances are manifested and can be analyzed and worked through.

Howard Bacal  

I am grateful to the editors of Psychoanalytic Inquiry for including me in their project to reconsider Franz Alexander's corrective emotional experience, since I believe the disrepute into which his idea has fallen is not entirely warranted. I contend that the main proposition it implies — that the significant therapeutic factor in psychoanalysis is an experiential one in the relationship between the patient and the analyst — is valid, although I disagree to some extent with the nature of the experience and the explanations for its validity.

In the first part of this paper, I discuss Alexander's views as well as those profferred by a number of other prominent psychoanalysts who also questioned the therapeutic exclusiveness of insight and studied the effectiveness of experiential factors in the analytic relationship. Following this, I elaborate my own perspective, which I have up to now outlined in previous publications (Bacal, 1985, 1988a, b; Bacal & Newman, 1990).

The term corrective emotional experience was introduced by Alexander and French (1946) and further elaborated by Alexander himself (1950, 1956, 1961) to account for the therapeutic effect of psychoanalytic treatment, whether this was classical analysis or its application in other forms of analytically oriented psychotherapy.

The Meeting of Needs in Psychoanalysis

Patrick Casement MA

Patrick Casement

122 Mansfield Road
London NW3 2JB9

Patrick Casement  

In this paper I wish to draw attention to some of the many ways in which needs from childhood recur in the course of analysis or therapy. A patient's re-presentation of need is, I believe, unconsciously in the service of a continuing search for attention to needs that have remained unmet.

First, however, I wish to remind the reader of a distinction that I regard as diagnostically essential in relation to the issue under discussion: that between “libidinal demands,” which cannot be gratified in any analytic psychotherapy without risking a serious disturbance of the analytic process, and “needs,” which cannot be frustrated without preventing growth. Winnicott (1960) has called these latter “ego-needs.” In relation to later development, I have found it useful to think of them as “growth-needs” (1985, pp. 170-172).

Superficially, it might seem that I am here advocating some form of “corrective emotional experience.” I wish to make it clear that this is not so, but I shall be linking what I am saying to the reexamination of that concept.

Patrick Casement is a training analyst of the British Psycho-Analytical Society, London. He is the author of On Learning from the Patient.

This paper is a revised version of a chapter in his forthcoming book Further Learning from the Patient (published by Routledge, London, 1990).

Anne Miller

Anne Miller  

Dr. Fosshage and his patient have a claim to our gratitude for their very valuable clinical material.

Our discussion will focus on two issues. The first is that of agency, of who is primarily responsible for the patient's difficulties; the second, subsidiary to this, concerns who is responsible for “damage” to the patient's objects. These issues were considered by most of our discussants.

The issue of agency was raised most sharply by Curtis as evidenced by the subtitle of his paper, “The Patient as Existential Victim.” Curtis is writing from the position of traditional psychoanalysis. A cornerstone of Freud's theory is the concept of psychic determinism. Addressing students, Freud wrote: “… you nourish a deeply rooted faith in undetermined psychical events and in free will, but … this is quite unscientific and must yield to the demand of a determinism whose rule extends over mental life” (1915-16, p. 106) If one takes the concept of psychic determinism seriously, then all patients, insofar as they are troubled, are victims. Whether one assumes, for example, that the patient's pathology stems from excessive inborn aggressive drives, or from inadequate parental responsiveness, or from a mix of these and other factors, the doctrine of psychic determinism dictates that, in each instance, the patient's feelings and behavior are determined.

Dr. Miller is Training and Supervising Analyst at the St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute, and Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at St. Louis University School of Medicine.

De Gustibus Disputandum: An Editorial Commentary

Stephen Post MD

Stephen Post

4524 Forest Park Boulevard
St. Louis, MO 63108

Stephen Post  

Psychoanalytic assessment, the basis for psychoanalytic science, takes place within an evolving interaction between two subjectivities at conscious, preconscious, and unconscious levels in ways that preclude any traditionally Cartesian distinction between observer and observed; each influences the other so that the discoveries made are heavily conditioned by the method of discovery. Much more obviously than in physics, there can be no certainty in psychoanalysis (see Coltart, 1986). For example, the once-fashionable analytic interpretation, “What you are experiencing is …,” followed by some specific of the analyst's certainty, relies on a scientific point of view long since superseded. Likewise with psychic determinism: absolute is obsolete. Our inclinations toward certainty can better be located in the expectation that both participants in a fruitful analysis will be changed by their encounter.

It may be impossible for anyone, howevermuch an outsider, to assess an ongoing psychoanalytic process without in some sense becoming a party to it. Our contributors to this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry are especially subject to such a liability, given their presence in the room by proxy via a tape recorder.

Dr. Post is a Training/Supervising Analyst and Chairman of the Education Committee of the St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute; he is Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at St. Louis University Medical School.

Epilogue

Jule Miller Issue Editor and Stephen Post Issue Editor

Stephen Post

Stephen Post  

The foregoing contributions by Dr. Fosshage and our discussants enable us to see the necessary and inevitable role that theory plays in clinical analysis — in data selection, in understanding, in analytic technique, and even in clinical perception. They also afford us glimpses of the inseparable mix of temperament and theoretical orientation that constitutes each clinician's way of working and thinking. In addition, they underscore the uniqueness of each patient/analyst “fit” — or lack of fit — and help us to appreciate the role of theory in this regard as well.

We are mindful that if we were to employ another self psychological clinical presenter, another patient, and other discussants from each of the points of view represented here, the results would be significantly different — if not necessarily incompatible. We are aware that we have only scratched the surface; there is much more to be learned from such experience-near studies of the interplay between theory and technique. A major beneficiary, as we can see here, will be the field of comparative psychoanalysis.

To us, these are exciting times in which to be working. Not only is the scope of analysis widening, but so also is the viewpoint of analysts. In the United States, with which we are most familiar, there have long been competing schools — Freudian, Jungian, Adlerian, Sullivanian, followers of Horney, etc. — largely out of communication with one another. That state mostly persists, at least from the Freudian side. But within the Freudian school there has been an evolution. During the middle decades of this century the dominant theoretical position was that of ego psychology, especially as articulated by Hartmann, Kris, Loewenstein, and Rapaport, with due respect paid to the writings of Anna Freud from abroad. Less attention was given to the Kleinians and other object relations theorists, although faint stirrings could be heard. Self psychology had not yet been conceived.

Addicted to drugs in the past, to alcohol and to promiscuous behavior, Dr. Fosshage's patient had become chronically depressed after her previous female analyst had consistently refused to let the patient know whether she (the analyst) “cared” about her. Psychotherapy as a Trial for Psychoanalysis

Leonard Horwitz PHD

Leonard Horwitz

Box 829
Topeka, KS 66601

Leonard Horwitz  

Astriking phenomenon in psychoanalytic literature is the relatively scant coverage of a process to which psychoanalysts are paying increasing attention: converting psychotherapy to psychoanalysis with the same treater. Only two articles have appeared specifically addressed to this topic and both have been recent (Bernstein, 1983; Levine, 1985). The reasons for the dearth of material on this subject are not entirely clear, but may be related to the relative infrequency of the procedure in the past. The last major survey of psychoanalytic practice (conducted by the American Psychoanalytic Association in 1976 [Shapiro, 1980]) revealed that 12 percent of the patients then in psychoanalytic treatment had seen their analysts first in psychotherapy. In contrast, 40 percent of this patient pool had had previous psychotherapy with a different analyst.

The recent proliferation of workshops, panels, and articles on this topic indicates that the 12-percent figure may be considerably higher today. Since the early 1980s the American Psychoanalytic Association has sponsored several discussion group on the subject, including a panel in 1983 (Panel, 1987), suggesting that the process of converting is a subject of much greater interest than it was heretofore and is unquestionably regarded as a boon to candidates and graduate analysts seeking psychoanalytic cases.

Dr. Horwitz is Training and Supervising Analyst at the Topeka Institute of Psychoanalysis.

Joseph Lichtenberg MD and L. Levi MD

L. Levi

1616 18th Street NW
Washington, DC 20009

L. Levi  

The subject of converting psychotherapy to psychoanalysis has long been beset by controversy. Often the argument has had a moralistic tone, such as preserving the pure gold of analysis and not contaminating the transference. Even “converting” has a religious flavor which “shifting” would not. The patient shifts from one form of treatment to another as a patient with back trouble shifts from bed rest to medication, exercise, or surgery. None of these connotations are important in themselves. Their only significance lies in whatever influence they have had in interfering with a consistent and careful study of this common clinical event. Current need demands such a study. If patients who have begun psychotherapy were to be eliminated as prospective analysands, everyone would suffer. Patients would be deprived of a possibly optimal treatment, and analysts and candidates would be deprived of both patients and a challenging experience, all because of unproven assumptions or unsubstantiated value judgments.

Dr. Lichtenberg, a member of the Faculty of the Washington Psychoanalytic Institute, is the Editor-in-Chief of this journal.

Nathan Schlessinger MD

Nathan Schlessinger

35 East Wacker Drive
Suite 3200
Chicago, IL 60601

Nathan Schlessinger  

The conversion from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis is a topic of formidable dimensions, engaging as it does, the perennial issue of defining the two modes of treatment in terms of theory and technique. Shifting definitions of psychoanalysis both as process and treatment have contributed to the complexity of the discussion.

In a survey on psychoanalytic practice, Shapiro et al. (1981) reported that one eighth of the analytic cases had previous psychotherapy. The numbers of psychotherapists have been increasing at an accelerating rate in the interim, and clinic experience at intake demonstrates an accompanying rise in frequency of previous psychotherapy among prospective analysands. Practically speaking, the “pure, uncontaminated” analytic case is apt to become an endangered species. Furthermore, there is a growing opinion (Panel, 1987) that some cases give positive indications for previous psychotherapy. The question, then, is, what theoretical and technical considerations determine an appropriate conversion.

In this paper, I consider the topic of conversion from psychotherapy to psychoanalysis in the broadest context, whether the conversion is conducted by the same analyst or after referral to another analyst.

Dr. Schlessinger is Associate Dean for Clinical Services, Institute for Psychoanalysis, Chicago; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, College of Medicine, University of Illinois.

Four Winds-Chicago

My reading of P's treatment narrative uses Lacan's distinctions among three dimensions of experience that he calls the Real, the Imaginary, and the Symbolic, dimensions that help to conceptualize the patient's “need” and to differentiate it from her demand and desire. These are salient issues in the case material insofar as Dr. F repeatedly uses the idea of “need” in his own reflections on the analytic process, and insofar as that process, as presented, operates for the most part in Lacan's dimension of the Imaginary. In so reflecting on the meaning of the analytic process, we are acknowledging that in the analytic moment itself we are likely to be governed by factors beyond conscious consideration, and that these factors have escaped both the analyst's and our retrospective efforts. This well-known caveat lies at the heart of Felman's (1987) brilliant rereading of Freud and Lacan.

Dr. F appears to respond to perceived “needs” in his patient by attempting to establish and reinforce a type of one-to-one reciprocal relationship in which mirroring and idealizations are prominent. From Lacan's perspective (1988) this amounts to a “two-body psychology” that excludes the mediating role of the unconscious and of the symbolic register as a third, as Other, to the dual, ego-to-ego-relationship.

Dr. Muller is Director of Psychotherapy/Psychology, Four Winds-Chicago.

It was 44 years ago, in 1946, that Franz Alexander published his pivotal thoughts on the corrective emotional experience and set in motion a fiery debate within psychoanalysis. Many of his colleagues thought that Alexander was diluting psychoanalysis and squandering the gains painfully won over the decades since Freud first began his pioneering investigations. Typical of the majority view of psychoanalysts was the comment that Alexander and his group were perhaps doing good psychotherapy, but that it was not psychoanalysis. So great was the ferment aroused by Alexander as well as other analysts bent on modifying the traditional classical conceptualizations that, in 1954, an entire issue of the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association was devoted to a discussion of these controversies. The majority view at that time, represented by Bibring, Gill, Rangell, and Stone, critically disagreed with Alexander. As a consequence the phrase corrective emotional experience became a symbol for a not quite psychoanalytic therapy from which reputable psychoanalysts usually tried to distance themselves.

Franz Alexander's original formulation of the corrective emotional experience consisted of the psychoanalyst's efforts to utilize the discrepancy between the expectations transferred from the past and the current behavior of the analyst. This emphasis is to be accomplished by interpreting the clinical transference.

The essence of the therapeutic process consists of the difference between the physician's reaction and that of the parents, parent substitutes and/or siblings. The objective nonevaluating attitude which has the emotional connotation of helpful interest is certainly a most significant factor revival in the transference situation. Equally important, however, is the recognition on the patient's part that these reactions are not suited to the analyst's reactions, not only because he is objective but also because he is what he is, a person in his own right…. This recognition is not merely intellectual insight, but is at the same time an emotional experience. Simultaneously recognizing and experiencing the discrepancy between the transference feelings directed toward the original objects in the past, and the reactions of the therapist, who is a distinct personality and is experienced as such by the patient, is what I called the corrective emotional experience [Alexander, 1958, p. 327].

Converting psychotherapy to psychoanalysis is relatively commonplace in today's psychoanalytic practice. There are still, however, a number of unresolved questions related to such a procedure. For instance, does the very fact of converting make the subsequent psychoanalysis more difficult or even impossible? If such a procedure takes place, should the patient be transferred to another therapist for the analysis? What are the essentials of psychotherapy and of psychoanalysis that have to be taken into account in such a conversion? For training purposes should conversion from psychotherapy, especially with the same therapist, be allowed for the required supervisory cases?

Many of these questions can be traced to Freud's papers on technique (1911-1915), particularly the following statement: “Lengthy preliminary discussions, … previous treatment by another method and also previous acquaintance between the doctor and the patient … result in the patient's meeting the doctor with a transference attitude which is already established and which the doctor must first slowly uncover instead of having the opportunity to observe the growth and development of the transference from the outset. In this way the patient gains a temporary start upon us which we do not willingly grant him in the treatment” (1913, p. 125).

I in a previous paper, written jointly with Anne-Marie Sandler (Sandler & Sandler, 1978), a number of ideas relating to the development of object relationships were considered, with special reference to the role of feeling states in that development. We pointed out that the term object relationship has a variety of meanings, and that there is a need to face the task of integrating the theory of object relationships into the intrapsychic psychology of psychoanalysis. We were critical of the notion of an object relationship as the energic investment of an object, and pointed out that the relationship between two people involved very subtle and complicated cues. Object relations theory directly confronts certain assumptions that are at the heart of Freud's basic ideas. Although all object relations theorists do not reject Freud's instinct or drive theory they all challenge Freud's view that the object can be simply defined as the aim of an instinct. I intend to focus here upon the problem of the concept of instinct itself, which highlights the controversy between object relations theory and “classical” theory. This controversy has a certain practical consequence as it influences our theory of treatment and our therapeutic strategies.

Fairbairn's rejection of instinct theory in favor of energized structures is the most radical alternative to Freud's tripartite model of the mind. Fairbairn (1952) viewed energy as inseparable from psychic structure. (p. 85) “‘Impulses’ cannot be considered apart from the endopsychic structures which they energize and the object-relationships which they enable these structures to establish; and equally, ‘instincts’ cannot profitably be considered as anything more than forms of energy which constitute the dynamic of such endopsychic structures.”

So say whatever goes through your mind. Although analysts differ regarding which factors are essential to psychoanalysis, free association is generally agreed to be a central aspect of the psychoanalytic process.
